strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and recognized limitation of Quality-Diversity optimization: reliance on hand-crafted behavioral descriptors, which constrains exploration and requires domain expertise.

The approach is theoretically grounded: embedding occupancy measures via Random Fourier Features to approximate MMD is principled, and Theorem 1 (with a full proof in the appendix) provides a high-probability guarantee that embedding distances approximate true MMD distances between occupancy measures, with error decaying in both samples (n) and features (D).

Clean, practical algorithm design: the random-feature embedding, the variance-reduction trick (Eq. 6), the fitness-weighted PCA, and the calibration step are all well-motivated, and the method integrates seamlessly with off-the-shelf QD optimizers (CMA-MAE) rather than requiring a bespoke learning pipeline.

Strong empirical evaluation: six standard continuous-control environments, five relevant baselines spanning distinct strategy families (hand-crafted BDs, autoencoder-based AURORA/LSTM-AURORA, population-diversity DvD-ES, skill-discovery RL SMERL), and method-agnostic evaluation metrics (Vendi Score and quality-weighted Vendi Score) that avoid hand-designed descriptors.

Useful additional experiments: robustness to changed dynamics (friction/mass) demonstrating a concrete benefit of diverse populations, plus ablations on embedding and descriptor dimensionality showing robustness to the embedding dimension and a clear quality-diversity trade-off in descriptor dimension.

Honest treatment of failure cases (HalfCheetah sliding behaviors, Walker2d foot-joint overemphasis) and a candid limitations section discussing kernel bandwidth sensitivity, sample efficiency in stochastic environments, and scalability constraints inherited from grid archives.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest: the core result is essentially a corollary of known random Fourier feature concentration results (Rahimi & Recht, Sec. 3 of [34]) combined with Hoeffding's inequality. The proof also contains some looseness (e.g., informal O(1/n) bookkeeping in Eq. 14-17 and crude bounding in Eqs. 34-36).
Only three random seeds for the main comparisons; with high-variance QD/RL experiments, this limits statistical power, and some reported gaps (e.g., HalfCheetah qVS) are within or near noise ranges.

The evaluation kernel for the Vendi Score is built on RFF embeddings over state-action pairs. Despite using a separate feature set, this choice structurally favors methods that optimize occupancy-measure diversity (AutoQD) and may disadvantage autoencoder-based baselines; a fully method-agnostic behavioral similarity would strengthen the diversity claims.
Ablation studies are conducted only on BipedalWalker; generalization of conclusions about descriptor/embedding dimensions to other environments is unverified.

Results are not uniformly dominant: AutoQD underperforms on HalfCheetah qVS and Walker2d VS/qVS, and the paper's qualitative explanations (sliding gaits, overemphasis on feet joints) suggest the learned descriptor space can miss behaviorally interesting dimensions.

Scope is limited to low-dimensional state-action observations; applicability to image-based or high-dimensional observations is deferred to future work, as is integration with gradient-based QD methods for sample efficiency.

Minor presentation issues: a duplicated reference ([8] and [9] are identical), a typo in Sec. 3.1 ('in practice, we ψπ as defined...'), and reliance on several somewhat ad-hoc hyperparameter choices (fixed kernel width, discount factor γ=0.999, update schedule) with limited sensitivity analysis beyond the dimension ablations.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: removing hand-crafted behavioral descriptors is a recognized and important limitation of QD optimization, and the occupancy-measure/MMD framing is a principled way to define behavioral similarity.

The main technical result (Theorem 1) provides a finite-sample convergence guarantee connecting the practical embeddings to true MMD distances between occupancy measures, giving the method more theoretical grounding than prior unsupervised-QD approaches (e.g., Aurora, TAXONS).

The experimental comparison covers five relevant baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL) representing distinct strategies, uses a shared underlying QD optimizer for fairness, and includes a dynamics-adaptation application demonstrating a practical benefit of diverse populations.
The appendices are thorough: full proofs, complete cwPCA details, CMA-MAE pseudocode, and extensive hyperparameter tables improve reproducibility.
Ablation studies on embedding dimension and descriptor dimensionality provide useful insight, e.g., the robustness to RFF dimension and the quality/diversity tradeoff as descriptor dimension grows.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the evaluation: the Vendi Score and qVS kernels are constructed from RFF embeddings whose geometry the authors justify via their own theory. Since AutoQD directly optimizes to spread policies along exactly this kind of embedding, its diversity may be inflated relative to methods optimizing different similarity notions, making the headline diversity metrics not fully method-agnostic as claimed.

Only three random seeds per algorithm-environment pair. Several comparisons (e.g., HalfCheetah qVS where Aurora wins, Walker2d qVS/VS where RegularQD wins) show overlapping or small margins, and the large standard errors in Table 1 make many of the 'consistent improvements' claims statistically fragile.

The theoretical contribution is incremental: Theorem 1 is essentially a composition of standard results (Rahimi-Recht uniform convergence of random features plus Hoeffding bounds), and the estimator actually used in practice (ψπ, Eq. 6) deviates from the i.i.d. sampling assumption analyzed in the theorem without a matching guarantee.

The gap between theory and practice is also visible in design choices that are heuristically motivated rather than analyzed: fixed kernel bandwidth, fitness-weighted PCA, and 5th/95th percentile calibration. No sensitivity analysis is given for the kernel width, which the authors themselves list as a limitation.

Performance is mixed on two of six environments: AutoQD underperforms on qVS in HalfCheetah (discovering diverse but low-quality 'sliding' policies) and on VS/qVS in Walker2d. The qualitative explanations (visual inspection, 'overemphasized feet joints') are anecdotal rather than supported by quantitative analysis.

The evaluation scope is limited to six standard Gymnasium/MuJoCo locomotion tasks with low-dimensional states; claims about 'open-ended learning' and 'automated behavior discovery' are not tested in settings (high-dimensional observations, stochastic environments) where occupancy estimation would be hardest.

GT QD Score inherits hand-crafted descriptors, so the main quality metric partially favors methods whose notion of diversity aligns with the expert-defined behavior spaces; the interaction between this metric choice and the conclusions deserves more discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated limitation of QD algorithms: reliance on hand-crafted behavioral descriptors. Framing descriptors via occupancy measures gives the approach a principled foundation that distinguishes it from autoencoder-based alternatives like Aurora.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is a nice addition: it formally connects finite-dimensional random Fourier feature embeddings to MMD distances between occupancy measures, with a complete proof in the appendix combining Hoeffding bounds and the Rahimi-Recht uniform convergence result.

The experimental evaluation is comparatively thorough for this area: six continuous control environments, five diverse baselines spanning both QD-based and RL-based approaches, and three evaluation metrics including the method-agnostic Vendi Score and quality-weighted Vendi Score, which is a thoughtful way to handle the inherent difficulty of comparing methods that optimize different diversity notions.
The cwPCA design choices (fitness weighting, percentile-based calibration to fixed archive bounds) are well-motivated and clearly documented in the appendix.
A useful application experiment demonstrating robustness to changed dynamics (friction/mass variation), which supports the practical motivation for behaviorally diverse populations.
Reproducibility is strong: detailed hyperparameters, architectures, environment versions, computational resources, and ablations on embedding and descriptor dimensions are provided.
weaknesses: Only three random seeds per environment-method pair is statistically weak. Several of the reported gains (e.g., HalfCheetah QD score, Walker2d metrics) have overlapping or large standard errors, making it hard to assess whether differences are significant. Significance tests or more seeds are needed.

There is a potential evaluation bias concern: the Vendi Score and qVS are computed using Gaussian kernels over RFF embeddings of policies—the same type of representation used internally by AutoQD. Although the authors use a separate, larger set of features and the median heuristic, this choice could plausibly favor methods whose behaviors are well-separated in the RFF/occupancy-measure geometry. A complementary diversity metric on raw states/actions would strengthen the claims.
The main theorem, while correct, is a fairly straightforward composition of known results (Rahimi-Recht uniform convergence plus Hoeffding/Monte Carlo bounds), so the theoretical novelty is moderate.

The GT QD Score relies on hand-designed behavioral descriptors, which partially undercuts the headline claim of eliminating the need for such descriptors; methods are still being judged through hand-crafted behavior spaces.

Evidence of limitations in two environments (HalfCheetah sliding behaviors, Walker2d foot-joint overemphasis) is only via visual inspection and anecdotal discussion; a more systematic analysis of failure modes would be valuable.

Scope is limited to low-dimensional state-based continuous control with Toeplitz-parameterized policies; scalability claims (thousands of policies, complex domains) are asserted but not demonstrated, and no wall-clock or sample-efficiency comparison is given.
The kernel bandwidth is fixed and acknowledged as a sensitivity factor, but no ablation of its effect is provided.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: removing hand-crafted behavioral descriptors from QD-RL, a genuine limitation of the field.

Theoretically grounded approach: Theorem 1 provides a finite-sample probabilistic guarantee that embedding distances approximate true MMD between occupancy measures, and Appendix B carefully connects the theoretically analyzed estimator to the practical trajectory-based embedding (ψ) with an explicit additional error term.

The framing via occupancy measures is principled and distinguishes the work from prior descriptor-learning methods (Aurora, LSTM-Aurora) and unsupervised skill discovery (DIAYN, SMERL), and the related work section positions the contribution well.

Solid empirical evaluation: six continuous control tasks, five diverse baselines covering different strategies (hand-crafted BDs, autoencoders, LSTM encoders, ES-based diversity, RL-based skills), and three complementary metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, qVS) with thoughtful discussion of their biases.

AutoQD outperforms baselines on most environments and metrics, with honest analysis of failure cases (HalfCheetah sliding behaviors, Walker2d lower-joint overemphasis) rather than only favorable reporting.
Useful downstream application study: adaptation to changed friction/mass demonstrates practical value of diverse populations, with AUC and success-threshold analyses.

Extensive ablations in the appendix: weighting mechanism (with statistical testing), embedding dimension, descriptor dimension, number of rollouts, descriptor stability analysis, and qualitative behavior visualizations. Code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Only three random seeds for the main results, with large standard errors in some cases (e.g., HalfCheetah QD score 30.78 ± 2.72; Walker2d VS 8.4 ± 3.2); several comparisons may not be statistically robust, and the text makes no claims of significance testing for the main table.

Theoretical contribution, while correct-looking, is largely a composition of known results (RFF approximation of the Gaussian kernel, uniform convergence of Rahimi & Recht, Hoeffding/McDiarmid/Pinelis inequalities); the novelty of the analysis itself is moderate.

Evaluation is limited to low-dimensional state-based benchmarks (five MuJoCo tasks plus BipedalWalker); no image-based or higher-dimensional observation domains, which limits evidence for scalability claims, and the paper concedes this in limitations.

The claimed one-to-one correspondence between policies and occupancy measures technically holds for deterministic Markovian policies; distinct stochastic policies can share occupancy measures, so the statement that occupancy measures 'fully characterize a policy' is slightly overstated and relevant to the behavior-characterization motivation.
No sensitivity analysis of the kernel bandwidth σ, which the paper itself identifies as an influential design choice; the heuristic σ = sqrt(state dim + action dim) is used without justification.

Underperformance on two of six domains (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) is attributed to early convergence to stable behavioral modes, but no mitigation is attempted in this work, leaving a substantive open question about the method's exploration dynamics.

Blackbox optimization via CMA-MAE requires many environment evaluations; a direct sample-efficiency comparison against RL-based baselines (SMERL) is confounded by very different evaluation budgets, and this is not rigorously controlled.

Descriptor updates change the behavior space mid-optimization, which the authors note destabilizes gradient-based QD methods; compatibility with stronger QD optimizers (PGA-ME, PPGA) is deferred to future work, weakening the practical significance of the contribution.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: using occupancy measures, which are known to characterize Markovian policies uniquely, as the basis for automatically generated behavioral descriptors removes a significant manual-design burden in QD-RL.

The paper provides an explicit probabilistic guarantee (Theorem 1) that RFF-based embedding distances converge to true MMD distances between occupancy measures, with an accompanying derivation of the practical trajectory-based embedding ψ (Appendix B), which is more rigor than most unsupervised-QD baselines (e.g., Aurora, DvD) offer.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: six continuous-control environments, five diverse baselines spanning QD and unsupervised-RL approaches, an application to dynamics adaptation, ablations over descriptor/embedding dimensionality, weighting, rollout count, and a descriptor-stability analysis.
Qualitative behavioral analysis (Appendix J) and the failure analysis for HalfCheetah/Walker2d are refreshingly honest and add interpretability. Source code availability supports reproducibility.
The paper is clearly written, with a clean algorithm presentation and detailed hyperparameter documentation.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Random Fourier features for approximating Gaussian-kernel MMD (Rahimi & Recht, 2007) and behavior embeddings of policies (Pacchiano et al., 2020; DvD; Chen et al., 2023) are all well established; the contribution is essentially their composition with CMA-MAE plus a fitness-weighted PCA. Theorem 1 is a fairly direct assembly of Hoeffding/McDiarmid concentration with the standard RFF uniform-convergence lemma, with loose constants and an abstracted O(·) term.

A fundamental evaluation concern: the Vendi Score and qVS metrics used to evaluate all methods are computed from a Gaussian kernel on RFF embeddings of occupancy measures—the exact same embedding family and distance that AutoQD explicitly optimizes over. Even with a separate, larger RFF set, this structurally favors AutoQD on the primary diversity metrics, and the fairness argument is asserted rather than demonstrated (e.g., by also reporting a metric defined in an independent space).

Only three random seeds for the main results is thin for RL/QD experiments with high variance (several entries have standard errors as large as the gap to the runner-up). Claims like 'AutoQD consistently outperforms the baselines' are not statistically supported; the paper's own ablation of fitness weighting (p > 0.7) concedes a key design choice is indistinguishable from noise.

There is tension in the narrative: the paper motivates itself by the limitations of hand-crafted descriptors, yet the primary metric (GT QD Score) is defined by hand-crafted BD archives, and the theory-justified embedding φ is replaced in practice by ψ, whose guarantee requires an additional (weaker-rate) bound and introduces finite-horizon truncation bias that is acknowledged but not carried through the final analysis.

Baseline strength is questionable. DvD-ES and SMERL perform near zero on most tasks (e.g., QD scores of 0.09–1.17 ×10^4 vs. AutoQD's 6–361 ×10^4), suggesting under-tuned or poorly adapted baselines rather than genuine comparisons; there is no comparison to DoMiNo, TAXONS, or other recent unsupervised-QD methods, and gradient-based QD (PGA-ME) appears only in the appendix, where it substantially outperforms the proposed method's optimizer.

Scope is narrow: all experiments are locomotion-style continuous control with linear/Toeplitz policies and evolutionary search. The acknowledged limitations (high sample cost in stochastic environments, early convergence to simple stable behaviors, fixed kernel bandwidth, incompatibility of descriptor refinement with gradient-based QD) are substantial and unaddressed, weakening the claim that this 'opens new possibilities for open-ended learning.'

The descriptor update mechanism (recomputing cwPCA on a schedule and remapping the entire archive) is a nontrivial nonstationary process that could distort archive semantics mid-run, yet its effect on convergence/stability of the QD search is not analyzed—only the update schedule is listed as a hyperparameter.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: removing hand-crafted behavior descriptors from QD optimization is a recognized limitation of the field, and the paper offers a principled, theoretically grounded solution based on occupancy measures and MMD embeddings.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 and the extension in Appendix B (covering the practical trajectory-based ψ embeddings and finite-horizon truncation bias) give a rigorous probabilistic guarantee connecting embedding distances to true MMD between occupancy measures, which distinguishes the work from largely heuristic prior approaches (Aurora, TAXONS, DvD).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: six continuous-control environments, five diverse baselines spanning QD, RL-based, and evolutionary diversity approaches, plus multiple metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, quality-weighted Vendi Score).

Strong main results: AutoQD outperforms baselines in most environments on both quality and diversity, and the adaptation experiments (friction/mass changes) demonstrate practical value of diverse populations beyond archive metrics.

Extensive supplementary analysis: ablations on descriptor/embedding dimensionality, fitness weighting, rollout count; descriptor stability analysis (Appendix I); qualitative behavior visualizations; honest discussion of failure cases (HalfCheetah sliding, Walker2d low-joint focus).
Source code is released and implementation details/hyperparameters are thoroughly documented, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical strength of the main comparison is limited: only three random seeds per environment-method pair, which is thin for claims of consistent superiority given the sizable variances (e.g., AutoQD's VS on Walker2d is 8.4 ± 3.2). The ablation in Appendix H/I uses three seeds on a single environment only.

Potential circularity in the diversity metric: the Vendi Score kernel is built from RFF embeddings structurally similar to AutoQD's own policy embeddings (albeit with a separate set). While the authors argue asymptotic equivalence to occupancy-measure MMD, the evaluation geometry may inherently favor the proposed representation over autoencoder- or LSTM-based baselines.

The theory analyzes i.i.d. sampling from the occupancy measure, but trajectories produce highly correlated state-action samples; the ψ-embedding analysis partially bridges this gap, yet the mismatch between assumptions and practice is not empirically validated (e.g., no verification that empirical embedding distances converge at predicted rates).

The theoretical result is largely an assembly of known tools (Rahimi-Recht uniform convergence, Hoeffding/McDiarmid inequalities, Puterman's policy-occupancy correspondence), so the novelty is primarily in the combination and application rather than fundamentally new theory.

Some baseline adaptations are non-trivial and could disadvantage them (e.g., SMERL hidden layers doubled, skills doubled, training steps changed; DvD-ES kept at author defaults with 10 policies), and all QD baselines use CMA-MAE rather than their originally published optimizers, complicating direct comparison to prior reported results.

AutoQD underperforms on two of six domains (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) due to early convergence to stable but simple behaviors; while honestly analyzed, the paper offers no mechanism to address this known failure mode.

Minor quality issues: duplicated identical references (Cully et al. 2015a/b), typos ('authros', 'difference were'), and the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('Source code is available at' with no URL).
